articles.title: SO Is Back! No, Not Stack Overflow, but Its Spirit
articles.summary:
One thing people complained about most on Stack Overflow was having their questions closed and marked as duplicates of other questions that were only slightly related. The poster would argue in the comments, trying to make the case that their question was different, only for it to fall on deaf ears.
Then LLMs came along and ate Stack Overflow's lunch. An LLM will answer your question, and with even more vigor if a related question exists online. Everyone was happy, until the LLMs suddenly stopped responding.
Along the way, we decided that LLMs are too dangerous and shouldn't answer every development question. If your prompt sounds, even vaguely, like you are trying to circumvent security, the model drops your request and flags your account. Do it enough times, and your account is closed for good.
Now it's no longer smug developers closing questions. You are left with an unanswered prompt and no one to pin the fault on.
Even when they don't blatantly stop you in your tracks, the answers can feel gated, as if the model knows the answer but deliberately won't tell you.
Now, I was never so much against marking questions as duplicates. In the majority of cases I encountered, the person asking could have benefited from reading the original question. You don't get a full answer, but it serves as a guide that helps you find a solution. With LLMs withholding answers, the fix is often to pay for a more expensive model. So maybe it's not so much Stack Overflow as ExpertSexChange that is back.

articles.title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
articles.summary:
Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook (https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com).
Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community.
Here’s a demo video: (https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM)
If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild.
We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do.
More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state).
Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862, August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449, May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code.
How it works…
Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal.
When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas.
The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant.
Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is.
This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt.
We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built.
The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams.
We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code!
The Onlook team (Joel - thebrubaker and Kris - krisodd), and I will be here all day!

articles.title: Inside PyPy: first contact with RPython
articles.summary:
I get restless now and then and I want to implement a programming language.
Then after mustering the resolve, I stew, for there is no good implementation
language.1 What am I to do, build my own programming language so
that I can then use it to implement the first language? So I go back to
modifying an existing implementation instead.
There do exist established general-purpose tools for building fast programming
language implementations:
RPython, which has PyPy (Python) as its primary success story but also can
claim Topaz (Ruby) and a couple of other smaller ones
Truffle, which is the foundation of TruffleRuby, GraalPython, GraalJS, and
even Sulong (LLVM)
And more nascent ones such as Deegen, which was used to reimplement Lua.
They each take different approaches:
Deegen requires you to write your bytecode interpreter and type system in a
C++ DSL. From this it generates an interpreter, a baseline JIT compiler, and,
hopefully eventually, an optimizing JIT compiler.
Truffle requires you to write an AST or (newly) bytecode interpreter in an
Annotation-based Java DSL. From this it specializes guest language code
before emitting Graal IR, which uses aggressive partial evaluation to
generate optimized code.
RPython requires you to write an interpreter in a restricted dialect of
Python 2 that acts more like Java or Go than Python. The RPython compiler will then
analyze your code, translate your “Python” program into C code bundled with
RPython IR, and then “tier up” from the C code to JITed code at run-time. In
order to go from “random RPython program” to “JIT compiler”, you need to
participate in its meta-tracing, which requires annotating where your
interpreter loop loops.
While none of these spark joy, they do each have benefits, including
accomplishing the primary goal of offloading a lot of the language runtime
choices and nasty details.
In this post we will take a first look at RPython because it is the kind of
VM implementor’s programming language that I keep thinking about. More on that
later.
Before we continue, please heed this warning: RPython is an implementation
detail of PyPy. It has not had the years of polish that the rest of the system
has had. Please do not badger maintainers.
A little Python
We’re going to build a little program in RPython. I am mostly following along
with the docs, specifically
Getting Started with
RPython.

# double.py
def double(x):
    return x + x

def entry_point(argv):
    print double(3)
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    sys.exit(entry_point(sys.argv))


There’s a little more ceremony than you might be used to and that’s because
we’re going to run this file in two modes: normal Python 2 interpreter and
compiled to C. This is the weirdness of RPython.
Run it:

$ python2 double.py


If you don’t have python2 installed, you can install PyPy, which helpfully
still implements Python 2.
If this all went fine, you will see it print 6.
None of this is RPython yet. For that, we need a hint more ceremony.
First contact
This is when we clone the PyPy project, in which we will find RPython.

$ git clone --depth=1 https://github.com/pypy/pypy


Now edit the Python program. Below the entry_point definition, add the
following function:

def target(*args):
    return entry_point


This target function looks unused, but it is actually a hint to RPython: this
is where the compiler should start translating.
Let us now compile this program. Either inside the PyPy directory or with
PYTHONPATH=/path/to/pypy, run:

$ python2 /path/to/pypy/rpython/bin/rpython double.py


If all goes well, you will see a whole mess of output, including a partially
rendered Mandelbrot fractal. Finally, you will see something like:

...
[Timer] Timings:
[Timer] loading target                 ---  0.0 s
[Timer] annotate                       ---  0.5 s
[Timer] rtype_lltype                   ---  0.5 s
[Timer] backendopt_lltype              ---  0.3 s
[Timer] stackcheckinsertion_lltype     ---  0.0 s
[Timer] database_c                     --- 10.6 s
[Timer] source_c                       ---  1.2 s
[Timer] compile_c                      ---  1.5 s
[Timer] =========================================
[Timer] Total:                         --- 18.0 s
$


This is the RPython compilation process. In it, RPython is analyzing types,
removing memory allocations, monomorphizing functions, and generating C code.
Then it hands this C code off to a C compiler to compile.
You should have in your current directory an executable named double-c, which
you can run like ./double-c. It should also print 6.
So far, this is not so different from Python. But let’s try something Pythonic.
Let’s see what happens when we also use + to mean string concatenation.

def double(x):
    return x + x

def entry_point(argv):
    print double("a")
    print double(3)
    return 0

def target(*args):
    return entry_point

if __name__ == "__main__":
    import sys
    sys.exit(entry_point(sys.argv))


Under normal Python 2, this will work just fine, printing aa and then 6.
Under RPython, though, you get this inscrutable error (again, rough edges):

[translation:ERROR] UnionError:

Offending annotations:
  SomeChar(const='a', no_nul=True)
  SomeInteger(const=3, knowntype=int, nonneg=True, unsigned=False)


Occurred processing the following simple_call:
  function double <double.py, line 1> returning

    v2 = simple_call((function double), (3))

In <FunctionGraph of (double:4)entry_point at 0x59c0ad837b40>:
Happened at file double.py line 6

        print double("a")
==>     print double(3)

Known variable annotations:

Processing block:
 block@6[argv_0] is a <class 'rpython.flowspace.flowcontext.SpamBlock'>
 in (double:4)entry_point
 containing the following operations:
       v3 = simple_call((function double), ('a'))
       v4 = str(v3)
       v5 = simple_call((function rpython_print_item), v4)
       v6 = simple_call((function rpython_print_newline))
       v2 = simple_call((function double), (3))
       v7 = str(v2)
       v8 = simple_call((function rpython_print_item), v7)
       v9 = simple_call((function rpython_print_newline))


and are unceremoniously dropped into the debugger, Pdb (hit Ctrl-D or type
exit).
From this message you are meant to intuit that RPython did not enjoy that two
different types flowed into the double function. It helpfully tells you that
there was a UnionError when trying to reconcile the SomeChar and
SomeInteger types that flowed into the function’s first parameter. It then
gives you a pointer to the offending line and an IR dump.
This happens because RPython requires function parameters to be monomorphic.
Though the variables are syntactically untyped, RPython computes a type
analysis to discover what type each variable should be. When "a" and 3 both
flow into x, boom, complaint.2
To get around this, we do what all good C++ programmers do and we templatize
the function. The RPython spelling of this is, as with many other features, a
function annotation:

from rpython.rlib.objectmodel import specialize

@specialize.argtype(0)
def double(x):
    return x + x

# ...


You will find now that RPython happily compiles the program. This works because
it makes a new copy of double for every input type of the first (0)
argument.
“Hey wait a minute,”, you might ask, “doesn’t this mean it stops being a valid
Python 2 program?”
Great question. No.
You can still run the program as long as you provide the location of the
RPython libraries via PYTHONPATH (as before):

$ PYTHONPATH=/path/to/pypy pypy double.py
aa
6
$


This runs ~instantly, which is a big relief. Developing an interpreter project
with a 30 second or more turnaround time for each compile would be really
frustrating.
This has been a taste of RPython, both great and somewhat frustrating. I
intentionally made it about RPython as a programming language rather than
being so focused on RPython as a programming language implementation tool
because I want some of its features to exist in a general purpose programming
language… that then also might be used to implement other programming
languages.
I bring it up because I want to rehash the stuff that I occasionally grumble
about in the vicinity of PLDI but for some reason have not written about
online. Perhaps writing about it will encourage people.
A new (meta-)programming toolkit
I think there is a lot of good stuff in RPython:
Compile to native AOT with additional JIT. Seems like this provides good
start-up performance with (optional!) tier-up as the runtime system observes
the system’s behavior.
Automatic memory optimization. There is no good way to syntactically express
how an object should be allocated—Python is, after all, a very high-level
language—so Python programs are profligate allocators of memory. RPython
programs would be the same except that the AOT compiler does a
whole-program analysis to try and remove these allocations. The JIT does too,
but via a different mechanism.
The JIT is provided to you. You don’t have to think about program analysis;
the PyPy authors think about it for you.
It is possible to do manual memory layout via lltype so that you can write
better data structures than Python would otherwise let you express.
It provides a garbage collector for you. Furthermore, it handles all the
stack scanning stuff and “oop maps” so you don’t have to build
handles/GC_PROTECT/… yourself.
I wish some stuff were different, or at least modifiable:
RPython does its partial evaluation and automatic JIT creation via
meta-tracing. It is one of the last surviving tracing JIT compilers
(alongside LuaJIT and, kind of, HHVM). For a lot of programs, method-based
compilers seem to have produced better, or at least more predictable,
results. I kind of want to see what a meta-method-JIT would look like.
The user experience leaves something to be desired. I want better error
messages, faster compiles, and less output. I want thorough docs.
I want better performance feedback. This is in line with the rest of my
ramblings about mechanical sympathy: the runtime should tell you what is
wrong. I (or CF) shouldn’t have to stare at IR in traces and go “hmmmmm…”
It requires writing a lot of your tooling anew. Even if I had, for example, a
JavaScript parser written in Python, it likely wouldn’t be in Python 2 and it
likely would not work well with RPython’s special rules. Runtimes such as
JRuby get around this by compiling parsers (Prism) to WebAssembly and then
bundling a WebAssembly interpreter written in Java.
Along these lines, I would like more help with lexing and parsing, for which
I have so little patience.
I think it would be neat if it had a way to pause and save an “image” of the
heap. After all, RPython is in control of all the memory and the code.
It would be neat if, in addition to a JIT, it also helped you build an AOT
compiler for your guest language.
What if your language is statically typed? Should the toolkit provide
functionality for type checking? Type inference?
Some solution for C code. You can call it and stuff just fine but there’s no
Sulong equivalent so it’s a totally opaque barrier to optimization. Don’t
write your runtime helpers in C, sure, but at some point you have to interact
with outside code.
I will probably add more to this list as I continue to remember some years of
these conversations.
Wouldn’t this be great?
Now what?
I don’t really have the time, energy, or expertise to build such a thing. There
are so many design decisions along the way. It would probably accidentally grow
to be huge and ossify along the way, and what a bummer that would be.
If you have any pointers to existing projects or a way to implement such a
thing in a really lightweight form (read: sub 10k lines, portable ideas), I
would be very interested.
Here are some pointers to other projects in the neighborhood:
Weval, which turns an interpreter into a baseline AOT compiler. Its current
implementation requires the interpreter to be compilable to Wasm and then its
heap snapshottable with Wizer. One can imagine this technique being used
instead to implement a JIT instead of an AOT, thereby also sidestepping the
snapshot requirement. One might also imagine this applying to another IR than
WebAssembly. Say, LLVM…
Yk, which is another tracing framework that you can add to an existing
interpreter. It traces and optimizes LLVM IR.
semPy, which is an executable semantics for Python.
Zig and other languages such as the more nascent k1 have the ability to run
and generate code at build-time. Perhaps someone could implement a VM toolkit
in one of these languages. I think a lot of the effort would still go toward
something like GC handles if you want a moving GC.
Virgil
Mojo
Thank you
Thanks for CF Bolz-Tereick first for allowing me to talk their ear off about
this for years and second for reviewing this post.
I don’t want to implement atop Racket. C++ and C give me endless
nightmares and are completely DIY. Yes, yes, I have built large VMs on C++
and C before. One time I posted so hard about the frustration that my tech
lead unfollowed me on Twitter. I don’t really want to try to think about GC
in Rust. ↩
I initially thought any variable had to be monomorphic but I
could not get an error from programs such as x = "a"; x = 3. ↩

Google is rebranding its Spark AI agent as “Tasks” and making
it free to use. The feature, which is powered by Google’s new
Gemini 4 Hydrogen AI model, can do things like create meal plans,
manage your calendar, and dig through your emails to find
recurring expenses you might not need.
Users in the US will get access to a few other features, including
the ability for the AI agent to call businesses to compare product
pricing and check inventory, purchase items with Google Pay, and
sign into accounts that support Google Password Manager. US users
can also assign Gemini tasks by emailing gemini@google.com or
texting it.
New rule for Google: measure twice and cut once when naming anything. Is there a single product they’ve come out with related to AI that hasn’t gone through at least two entirely different names? articles.title: Unburden yourself of the backlog
articles.summary:
David Marquet was a submarine commander who was abruptly assigned to work on a
boat he had no training on, and no idea how it worked. To compensate for his
lack of technical knowledge, he adopted a transparent leadership style, which
allowed the competence of the rest of the crew to fill in for his gaps.





During this process, he discovered that transparent leadership produced outsize
performance improvements compared to the more traditional leadership style of
the Navy. You should read the book he wrote about this experience. It’s well written and says
many good things.





There’s one thing in particular I keep coming back to all the time. In
the following transcription, I have snipped out some unrelated flavour to get to
the core of the chapter.






On board Santa Fe (152 days to deployment)



In addition to observing the ship perform its tactical manoeuvers, the
inspection team also looks at administrative issues. In this case, they
identified that Santa Fe had not responded to several messages we owed to the
squadron, SUBPAC, and the maintenance facility.



I asked the XO about the missed items, and he brought out the “tickler”, a
three-inch binder maintained by his yeomen that had all of the messages – such
as this one – that we received. They were sorted by department and due date. He
looked in the book and proudly reported that, sure enough, we were tracking this
particular message and knew we hadn’t responded.



So we had a system that was focused on understanding the status instead of
actually getting the work done. Unfortunately, everyone was too busy to look at
the binder, and in any event, it was stuck up in a locker in the XO’s
stateroom. Like every other submarine we would have weekly tickler meetings
where the department chiefs and department heads would sit in the wardroom for
an hour or more going through the binder page by page. Of course, none of this
activity actually resulted in getting any of the work done; it simply allowed us
to catalogue what we were supposed to do, and what we were delinquent on. It
sucked up a lot of time, valuable supervisory time.



This was how everyone did it, always had.



There is no requirement to maintain a tickler, only a requirement to get the
work done. We set out to invent an even more efficient way to do it, a new way.



The discussion went like this.



“Weps, who’s responsible for your department?”



“I am, Sir.”



“Not the XO?”



“No.”



“Then why should he spend time keeping a tickler for you and have you sit in all
these agonising tickler meetings?”



“He shouldn’t.”



“Okay. But here’s the deal: you guys need to get the work done.”



“We will.”



Weapons Officer Chief David Steele reminded me that his department had worked
through the night while we were in San Diego so we could participate in the
battle group-wide exercise. What I didn’t know was that Chief Steele had box
seats at the Padres game and had given those up. No one told him he had to do it
or ordered him to do it. It was needed to support the mission and he just did
it.



“So here’s what we are going to do. You are all going to monitor your own
departments and whatever is due. You are responsible, not me and not the XO,
for getting it done.”



And with that, we unburdened ourselves of the effort of maintaining the tickler.



This had two advantages. First, it would be more efficient because the work
would be getting done without the overhead of maintaining the tickler and those
darned tickler meetings. Second, there would be no illusion about who was
responsible for the performance of the various departments: the department heads
were!



Sure, I was worried that a lot of stuff would slip through the cracks and Santa
Fe would get a reputation for not getting the work done, but that didn’t happen.
I won’t say that we never again received a message zinging us for not reporting
something, but they were easily remedied and not that important. What was
incredibly powerful was the idea that everyone was responsible for their own
performance and the performance of their departments; that we weren’t going to
spend a lot of effort telling them what to do.

articles.title: Closing The Sandwich Shop
articles.summary:
As another media-industry stalwart shuts down, it remains essential for media outlets to control their own destinies.

Today, as Anthropic’s AI takes over the stock market, it’s more than a little weird to write a little lament to the way the internet once was.
But we recently lost Salon, one of the few news sites that’s been here more or less the entire time. And the reason cited sounds quite familiar:

The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable.

I’m sure that’s certainly true. But I also know that Salon has likely hit more of those road bumps than most. When it started, it was a site build around news, yes, but also a robust comments section. Then it gave that up, willingly. As I wrote in an aside earlier this year:

A testament to its legacy: Salon used the software as the anchor of its digital community for more than 15 years, only shutting it down in 2011 out of concerns it wasn’t where the Web was going. With another 15 years of retrospect, can we argue that this was probably a bad move? Perhaps.

I don’t want to argue prescience, but I do think decisions like these, where we handed off the infrastructure of our own destines to other companies in hopes that maybe they’d have a better idea than we would? They ultimately cost us necessary momentum and foundational strength.
Salon, as it looked in 1997.
The thing is, media outlets like Salon, which got its initial seed funding from Apple and Adobe (and Adobe continued to financially support for years after its launch), have long been swimming upstream. It had to ride a series of technology trends (search, social, video) to stay afloat. It wasn’t like Salon had originated any of these; it had to survive on the back of a tech ecosystem that saw financial opportunity in journalism, but not enough to build around it forever.
(It’s not like Adobe has invested millions of dollars in Salon anytime recently, after all. Free idea, Adobe: Maybe do that. Would be a great goodwill opportunity, considering the creatives you’ve frustrated of late.)
It’s freaking dark to kill a website immediately after an election that was deeply successful, given the website’s editorial viewpoint.
Matt Wolfbridge, the editor of the great Typebar Magazine which I’ve contributed to in the past, wrote a loving, but honest, take about where Salon went. He arrived there after its initial heyday, the period that gave us Joan Walsh and later Glenn Greenwald. While he was there, he grew its social presence in a big way. He didn’t hide its flaws, but he did note how much he loved the thing:

Everyone was happy for me when I did leave Salon for a surging news startup, which I did with a degree of sadness. Salon was the first thing in my professional life that had ever gone right. And it was staffed by many brilliant people whose devotion to the written word was so great they put up with the ownership’s demands. I am grateful for the time I spent there.

I didn’t work at Salon. I can’t claim any sort of institutional knowledge of what was there, like Matt can. But what I can say is that stuff like this makes me endlessly sad.


Soon, every digital news website you like will be owned by a company whose corporate website looks like this. (Find.co screenshot)
Salon’s late-stage owner: A reflection of 31 years of pivots?
Salon, in its own way, has reflected all the good and bad trends of digital-first journalism over the past 31 years. The most recent trend it reflected? The weird owner nobody who ever of, taking it over, Bending Spoons-style.
That’s right, Salon went down the same road that another great site in the internet’s digital legacy, Deadspin, did. It, too, was sold to a company based in Malta, with a background in iGaming, the shorthand term for “online gambling.” Salon, whatever its qualities before this shutdown happened, stuck out like a sore thumb in the context of Find.co’s product catalog.
“Leading Performance Marketing in Crypto” is not something one would associate with a long-running publication. But when I read “company that has crypto and iGaming interests buys website with 31 years of SEO juice,” I think to myself, “Oh, they want the Google ranking, not the outlet.”
I could be wrong. Maybe the Find.co folks are perfectly nice people who thought it’d be fun to make a bet on traditional journalism at a time when it seems like nobody else was.
But given the way that media brands get put through the wringer by both internal and external technology partners, it’s not hard to look at situations like these with a raised eyebrow. After all, today it’s Salon. Tomorrow, it could be another legendary site. The problem with building empires on the shared infrastructure of others is that they’re changing the infrastructure even if you don’t want them to. You’re forced to react to it at all times.
And sometimes, those companies don’t even know what the hell they’re doing, either. I’ve been following the recent SEO-website headlines with great interest after it came out that Google’s AI Mode, a search feature that the company heavily pushed onto its search engine, was less profitable than the old version of Google. And that has led Google to test minimizing it in searches. (Unfortunately, that doesn’t include the much-maligned AI overviews, but hey, at least &udm=14 exists.)
That’s telling. Like the infamous Facebook-driven pivot to video that was based on inflated data, an entire industry has been forced to leap based on bets that another company is making without knowing that what they’re doing is actually working.
Wawa corporate wants to convince an entire generation of our best and brightest that they make heartless corporate decisions. All they have to do is keep this location, near William & Mary, open! (Aaron F. Stone/Flickr)
What a legendary Wawa can teach you about top-down decision-making
Recently, I was on the home page of The Virginian-Pilot, a paper where I once helped start a free daily newspaper, reading about how a community was protesting in an attempt to save a beloved Wawa location. The story I think offers a neat parallel for the challenges journalism faces. This location meant a lot to the students of William & Mary, but Wawa wants more stores with attached gas stations. Classic example of making a 30,000-foot decision without looking at what’s happening on the ground.
Clearly a struggling location with no foot traffic. It must close. (Sarah Ross/Flickr)
The tech industry is full of decisions like these, where bold bets are made at a high level without understanding where the value equation actually lies. Our latest initiative requires us to strategically pivot towards gas stations, so we must stop serving 19-year-olds who want a hoagie in the middle of the night. We need to push people towards AI so we keep them on site longer, so we hurt all the symbiotic relationships we created over the past 30 years.
At the bottom of the Pilot article, my eye was drawn to the fine print, presumably put there by the Tribune bosses:

The use of any content on this website for the purpose of training artificial intelligence systems, algorithms, machine learning models, text and data mining, or similar use is strictly prohibited without explicit written consent.

We are now past the point where media outlets are going to be nice about it. They’ve been burned way too many times. This top-down stuff is gonna cost us everything we actually care about if we don’t stop it.

Sandwiched Links
Shuffling alone: The website Solitaire Alone Together is both a compelling website and a statement on the loneliness epidemic gripping society. (↬ Jared Newman)

Listen, as lawyers go, Lowell “The Hammer” Stanley is as close as you’ll find to a real-life Saul Goodman. Which is why it’s shocking to learn that, like Goodman infamously once did, Stanley just had his law license suspended.
Just wanted to offer a quick shout to zsKnight, the developer of ZSNES, who has made an utterly charming game collection called Retro Endurance 8 Bit. The gimmick: The game keeps changing, channel-clicker style, as you rush through levels. (Think Action 52/UFO 50, but with a quirky sense of humor all its own.) Find it on Steam here.
--

articles.title: ★ Jon McCormack Retires From Apple
articles.summary:
Mark Gurman, reporting for Bloomberg today (gift link):
Jon McCormack retired at the end of October after more than eight
years at the company, according to people with knowledge of the
matter. He oversaw the Camera and Photos apps and the underlying
technology that determines how users capture, view and edit their
pictures and video.
Apple hasn’t named a new vice president to take over McCormack’s
exact role. Instead, his former deputies are assuming his
responsibilities under another executive, said the people, who
asked not to be identified while discussing internal moves. An
Apple spokesperson declined to comment.
His work included the redesigned selfie camera introduced with the
iPhone 17 lineup last year.
I’ve met McCormack a few times. He frequently led media briefings for new iPhone camera features. He was always thoughtful, insightful, and fair. Like, sometimes his demonstrations would involve comparisons between photos of the same subjects and scenes captured on iPhones and ones captured with flagship Android phones. The photos were all good. It was never “Here are some beautiful images captured on iPhones and some dogshit ones from a Samsung and OnePlus”. The differences were often subtle. He’d even make the case for why someone might prefer the Android ones. But he could explain why Apple — and he personally — preferred the ones from the iPhone. Not just how the iPhone camera captures and processes images, but why. He also knew when to let the images speak for themselves.
McCormack was deeply informed at a technical level. He reported directly to Craig Federighi and that level of engineering acumen showed. I can’t recall any question being too technical for him to have a ready answer. One of the best iPhone camera innovations in recent years is the redesigned Center Stage selfie camera introduced with the iPhone 17 (and Air) lineup last year. The square sensor is hardware, and McCormack was a software VP, but the feature exemplifies the way hardware and software are developed in tandem at Apple. McCormack was the public face for that feature — and internally, pushed to make it happen. That square sensor is bigger, which means (a) it’s more expensive; and (b) it takes up more space internally. Both of those require winning hard-fought arguments inside Apple in order to ship. The bottom line is that it helps iPhone users take better photos of themselves — and according to McCormack himself, over 1 billion selfies are taken with iPhones every day. The influence Apple’s Camera team has on the daily lives of billions of people is significant; McCormack understood that.
But what really struck me about McCormack, right from the start, is that he is clearly a serious photographer himself. That’s perhaps understating it. He recently published a book of his own nature and travel photography: Patterns: Art of the Natural World. He discussed the book in an hour-long interview with his Apple colleague Pamela Chen, whose job title is one of the coolest I’ve ever heard: Chief Aesthetics Scientist. (Chen, unsurprisingly, is also a talented photographer.)
Gurman:
His departure comes at a time when Apple is navigating a
fundamental shift in photography. Competitors such as Alphabet
Inc.’s Google and Samsung Electronics Co. have increasingly
embraced generative AI features that allow users to make
substantial changes to images. That has blurred the distinction
between capturing a real moment and creating an artificial one.
Two years ago in his iPhone 16 Pro review, returning to his repeated theme of “What is a photo?”, Nilay Patel quoted, at length, the answer he got from McCormack. I, in turn, quoted Patel quoting McCormack, and added:
McCormack’s response is genuinely thoughtful, and resonates deeply
with my own personal take. But it’s worth noting that Apple is the
conservative company when it comes to generative AI and
photography — and yet they’re still shipping Clean Up. I’m not
complaining about Clean Up’s existence. I’ve already used it
personally. I’m just saying that even Apple’s stance involves
significant use of generative AI.
This year, Apple added “extend” and “reframe” alongside Clean Up. I don’t love either of those features simply because I don’t like how they change the meaning of “What is a photo?”, but I don’t hate them either. We can’t put the generative AI genie back in the bottle. Apple, still, is the conservative company in the generative AI phone photography space.
Jon McCormack had a knack for shepherding good new features into the Camera app. But also, based on conversations I’ve had with multiple people who worked with him at Apple, McCormack was great at keeping stupid ideas out of the Camera app. Good new features that ship get more recognition than stupid new features that never ship — but the latter, I would argue, is the rarer and more important management skill. It’s far more important to keep stupid ideas out of any app than it is to add good new features. McCormack was the protector of the Camera app. Under his leadership, it remains focused on the craft and art of photography.
Lastly, everyone I know who worked with him loves the guy. McCormack was the perfect guy for an essential job, and he leaves big shoes to fill.

articles.title: My Least Favorite Example in Software Engineering
articles.summary:
I'm doing a lightning talk at Brooklyn Web Workers on 11/30! If you're in the area, come check it out. If you're not in the area (like 99.90% of the world), you can just read this newsletter instead.
As you probably know, I am obsessed with examples. Really, really, really obsessed with examples. The best examples should at least:
Be simple enough to understand
Clearly showcase the topic under discussion
Actually correspond to how the topic manifests in the real world
Give some rough idea on how to find other examples in the same vein
Basically, the example needs to both help the student understand the topic and also why the topic matters. If not to them, at least to someone they know.
A good example of a good example is demonstrating type safety with option types, which ensure that you always handle nulls in your program. It's intuitive, clear, and simple, and it shows why and how this would be useful in practice.
But I'm not here to talk about good examples.
I'm here to talk about bad examples
Specifically my least favorite example. Property-Based Testing is a testing approach where we generate random inputs to a program and check the outputs all satisfy some property. And like half the PBT introductions online use this same example:
test reverse-reverse:
    l = random_list()
    reverse(reverse(l)) == l



I hate this example because 1) I see it every-freakin'-where, and 2) it fails the "this topic matters" criteria hard. It gives you some idea of what property-based testing is, but doesn't give you any way to relate it to actual real-world testing. I mean, who writes list reversal algorithms for their job?1
And sure, common examples of regular testing like add(1, 2) == 3 are also useless, but 1) regular testing is mundane and you can probably figure out more useful tests from that 2) most people can give you better examples than that! PBT, on the other hand, is quite exotic for most people and they need a lot of guidance on how to go from "learning about the concept of properties and generators" to "testing real software". It's dying for really good example, but double-reversal and similar are all ya get.
I blame John Hughes for this

Why do we use this example in the first place? I propose two reasons.
It's a really easy example to remember and share, unlike more useful and interesting examples, which often add complexity. It's also language agnostic, which should really be a separate reason but is logically kinda the same as "easy".
The first guy to talk about PBT used it and everybody followed his example.
The first guy in this case is John Hughes and Quickcheck. He opened his paper with reversing a list twice and the rest is history.
(He had some other examples but they quickly got into the weeds of example generation and domain-specific properties. See reason one for why double-reversing is popular.)
I shouldn't blame John Hughes for this
That's the useful part of the lightning talk. There's one more thing I want to try covering if I have time, though: While John Hughes was the guy who introduced PBT, he was not the first guy to use the double-reverse example! Zohar Manna used the example in Inductive Methods for Proving Properties of Programs and Boyer and Moore (yes, that Boyer and Moore) used it in Proving Theorems about LISP Functions. Richard Bird and Philip Wadler also used the example in their book Introduction to Functional Programming (pg 68). So it was probably already a standard example that John Hughes took.
I'll observe that Manna/Boyer/Moore/Bird/Wadler used double-reverse as an example of how to prove things, while Hughes used it as a property to test. An example can be good in one context and bad in another.
I'll also note that Hughes did a lot of work on efficient functional representations of lists, so verifying double-reverse was a useful application to his context. It's not his fault everybody else in PBT ran with it.
And to be absolutely clear, he didn't have any kind of ethical responsibility to "pick a better example". It does demonstrate what PBT is. It's just not a useful example, and I really value usefulness in my teaching examples. Prolly more than most people tbh.
Anyway, that's roughly what I'm going to be talking about. If you've read this, you've probably seen most of the talk. I'm just going to be a bit rantier when I give it. Happy Thanksgiving to those of you who celebrate it!

articles.title: Pluralistic: How to forfeit one of copyright's best labor policies (19 Nov 2026)
articles.summary: Today's links How to forfeit one of copyright's best labor policies: Author beware, termination of transfer and loan-out companies don't mix! Hey look at this: Delights to delectate. Object permanence: History of interlibrary loan; Mike Pence v Hamilton; Snoopers' Charter is law; Teamsters transformed. Upcoming appearances: Oxford, Sheffield, Virtual, Oxford, Santa Barbara, Montreal. Recent appearances: Where I've been. Latest books: You keep readin' em, I'll keep writin' 'em. Upcoming books: Like I said, I'll keep writin' 'em. Colophon: All the rest. How to forfeit one of copyright's best labor policies (permalink) There's a seeming paradox to copyright. For 50 years (starting with the 1976 Copyright Act) legislatures have monotonically expanded copyright, so that today, copyright lasts longer, covers more works, restricts more activities, and provides for harsher penalties for infringement, all in the name of protecting artists. After 50 years of this, artists are, on average, poorer than we were in 1976, but the media companies we sell our work to are much, much richer. They're larger and more profitable, and yet our wealth (both in absolute terms and as a share of media company profits) has declined. This may feel like a paradox, but it's actually easy to understand unless you've had the self-inflicted neurological injury we call "getting an econ degree." That's an injury that leaves the sufferer incapable of reasoning about or even perceiving power. If you've avoided that fate, then you can see that when an artist sells to one of five publishers, four studios, three labels, two app companies or one ebook/audiobook company, that artist has very little leverage. In that market, giving an artist more to bargain with is just giving them more to bargain away. I have often compared giving more copyright to creative workers trapped in this oligopoly to giving a bullied schoolchild extra lunch money. No matter how much money you give that kid, they're not going to get fed. The bullies just take whatever money you give to the kid. Indeed, if you indirectly transfer enough money to the bullies, they'll pay for a global ad campaign: THINK OF THE HUNGRY SCHOOLCHILDREN! THEY NEED MORE LUNCH MONEY! This is exactly what has happened with 50 years of successive copyright expansions. Every time Congress gave a new copyright to creative workers, the cartels we bargain with just amended their non-negotiable contracts to force us to hand over that new right for no extra payment. Then they used those new rights to get richer and more powerful, and to exert more control over the distribution channels we need to reach our audiences, which made us poorer. Then Congress heard their THINK OF THE STARVING ARTISTS pitch, and gave us more copyright…which we promptly handed over to our bosses. Lather, rinse, repeat. If you want to feed a hungry schoolkid, you have to change the structure of the system. For example, you might open a credit account with the school lunchroom, so that the kid never has any cash for the bullies to take. Likewise, if you want to help artists get more money, you need to make a systemic change. There are lots of ways to do this. In 2022, Rebecca Giblin and I co-wrote a book called Chokepoint Capitalism, and we devoted half of the book to detailed, shovel-ready proposals for ways to alter the copyright system to benefit artists, not our bosses: https://www.beacon.org/Chokepoint-Capitalism-P2020.aspx That section includes a chapter on something called "termination of transfer," which was introduced with the 1976 Copyright Act. Under termination of transfer, any copyright contract (a "transfer") can be unilaterally canceled ("termination") by any creator after 35 years. So even if you sign away your copyrights for the entire term (your life plus 70 years), you can tear up that agreement after 35 years by notifying the company you sold your rights to and then filing some paperwork with the US Copyright Office: https://pluralistic.net/2021/09/26/take-it-back/ We got really excited about termination. For one thing, Rebecca is one of the world's leading experts on the subject. In 2021, she co-authored the landmark study "U.S. Copyright Termination Notices 1977-2020: Introducing New Datasets," published in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=3880708 Termination is a uniquely efficient way to make artists richer at the expense of our bosses. The fact that you can only exercise it after 35 years produces some very interesting effects. First, consider that almost no copyrighted works are commercially viable after 35 years (most copyrighted works cease to generate income after 14 years or less, this being the original term of copyright in the USA). The rare works that continue to generate revenue 35 years after their release are the "perennial favorites" that drive a vast share of media industry profits. Now consider that, between the realities of the human lifespan and the amount of time it takes most artists to master their craft, any given work you produced 35 years ago is almost certainly from the start of your career. That's the moment in which artists are typically most vulnerable. Artists at the start of their careers are unknown quantities and are often crammed into signing terrible deals, even worse than the "standard" media deal. Put these two facts together and you'll see that termination is disproportionately applicable to a body of work that is wildly profitable for media companies, but the creators of those works are entitled to even less of the money it generates, thanks to the crummy contracts they were railroaded into because they were just starting out when they made them. Termination lets creators cancel those crummy contracts, take back their rights, and bargain for a better deal with the old media company (or a new one). This time, they bargain from a position of unassailable strength, due to the fact that they're selling a property that's proven itself to be a perennial profit-generator. Best of all, you can't bargain out of termination. Even if you sign a contract that says, "I promise I will not exercise my termination of transfer right," you can still exercise your termination right. This is a structural change, like the parent who opens a charge account with the school cafeteria so that their kid no longer has any lunch money to hand over to the bullies. The way Congress wrote termination into the 1976 Act, it doesn't matter how hard the media company you initially sign with twists your arm, you literally can't promise them you won't use your termination right 35 years after signing. That's where that landmark study Rebecca co-authored comes in. Rebecca and her co-authors found that termination was working exactly the way Congress intended: it was making artists richer. It's particularly helpful to marginalized creative workers, for example, Black "heritage" musicians who were railroaded into terrible contracts that meant they never got a dime for decades of airplay, covers and samples of their hits. If this sounds familiar, you might be thinking of my 2024 technothriller The Bezzle, where I use this as a key plot point: https://us.macmillan.com/books/9781250865878/thebezzle/ Genre writers have really benefited from termination. The authors of massively popular YA series like The Baby-Sitters Club and Sweet Valley High claimed back their rights under termination. So did Peter Straub and Stephen King, who took back the rights to their early books and resold them on much more favorable terms. Just the threat of termination forced Disney to make giant payouts to Marvel's key creators, like Stan Lee, Steve Ditko and Jack Kirby: https://deadline.com/2023/12/marvel-court-termination-disney-spider-man-dr-strange-1234843941/ In Chokepoint Capitalism, Rebecca and I point out that most of the 1976 Copyright Act (like longer copyright terms) has failed to help artists, but termination is the rare exception, a proven effective way to put money in artists' pockets. Which is weird, because in the 50 years since the 1976 Act, Congress has repeatedly doubled down on pretty much every measure in the Act, except the one thing that is empirically proven to be good for artists. Of course, all that failed stuff in the 1976 Act is good for giant media companies, and termination is bad for those companies, so it's not hard to see why there's been so little legislative appetite to beef up termination. But it's also easy to see how we'd do that beefing up. In the original draft of the Copyright Act, termination was automatic, and kicked in after 20 years (meaning that 20 years after signing any contract, every creator would automatically get back all the rights they sold in the contract). The final version of the Act watered down termination so it kicks in after 35 years, and even then only after the artist does a ton of paperwork. Giving artists the termination rights they were promised in the initial draft of the 1976 Act is a no-brainer. But that's not what we've gotten from Congress. To the extent that Congress acted on termination, it was to take it away from musicians. In 1999, an obscure Congressional staffer named Mitch Glazier snuck a clause into an unrelated bill that made it impossible for most recording artists to exercise their termination rights. This was such a scandal that Congress had to convene a special session to cancel this amendment and restore musicians' rights, and Glazier was drummed out of his Congressional job: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Glazier#Work_for_hire Don't worry, Glazier landed on his feet: he was immediately hired by the RIAA (the record industry's lobbying arm) as their new CEO and there he perches even today, making more than $1.4m/year to do a job he continues to describe as "defending artists": https://projects.propublica.org/nonprofits/organizations/131669037 With Glazier as the standard-bearer for "artists' rights," it's no wonder that creators haven't gotten a better deal on termination out of Congress. Indeed, things are looking very bad for termination of transfer right now, thanks to a string of court decisions that pit a common tax strategy employed by freelance creatives against termination of transfer. Like many freelancers, creative workers often incorporate limited liability companies that contract with the companies that employ them. These companies then pass the revenue on to creators as "partner distributions." There are lots of reasons to like this arrangement: it simplifies probate and estate planning, helps creators fund their pensions, and offers tax deductions for expenses like a home office or research trips. This arrangement is especially common in Hollywood, where the companies that writers, directors, and other creative trades work through are called "loan-out companies" (because the company employs the creative, and "loans them out" to movie studios). Movie studios and other media companies have recently seized on the existence of these loan-out companies to argue (with a great deal of success) that the existence of these loan-out companies nullifies termination of transfer. You see, termination of transfer is only available for creative works that are independently produced and licensed through a copyright contract. Termination does not apply to "works made for hire," such as the emails and reports you might write in the course of your duties as an employee. The logic here is that termination of transfer is supposed to help artists get more out of their copyrights, but forcing (say) an insurance company to disgorge all the memos you wrote for them 35 years ago would introduce chaos and uncertainty without helping workers in any way (there's not exactly a market for 35-year-old insurance company memos). The media companies' argument goes that creative workers are employees of their loan-out companies, so if you sell a script or a novel through your LLC, that is a "work made for hire" that the LLC owned, and that means that it can't exercise your termination of transfer rights to get that work back after 35 years. Aaron Moss, who edits the Copyright Lately website, has been beating the drum about this for years, calling it "a ticking time bomb for copyright-intensive industries." He's been repeatedly vindicated, most recently through a bizarre dispute between Michael Mann, the director and writer of 1995's blockbuster Heat, and New Regency, the studio that released it: https://copyrightlately.com/michael-mann-heat-copyright-termination/ Moss's article on the dispute is a very entertaining read, unpacking a decidedly weird gambit that Mann has deployed to regain the rights to Heat. But the most important part of the article is the way it describes the state of play for termination's ongoing collision with loan-out companies. The studios and labels have racked up a string of wins using this gambit, with creators settling their cases or losing outright. Take musician John Waite's bid to get his rights back from UMG: the judge ruled in UMG's favor, saying, "people cannot use a corporate structure for some purposes – eg taking advantage of tax benefits – and then disavow it for others": https://copyrightlately.com/copyright-termination-loan-out-corporations/ This is a bad situation. Termination is a fantastic, artist-friendly legal doctrine, one that lets creators claim back some of our most cherished media. Termination gave George Clinton the rights back to his entire catalog (his sleazy ex-manager forged Clinton's signature on a rights assignment). It let Gary K Wolf take Roger Rabbit back from Disney: https://pluralistic.net/2025/11/18/im-not-bad/#im-just-drawn-that-way It let the Spinal Tap crew get a much better deal out of their studio, and paved the way for 2025's (criminally underrated) Spinal Tap II: https://www.nme.com/news/film/this-is-spinal-tap-creators-and-studiocanal-settle-rights-dispute-2757087 The Wachowskis just announced that they're going to exercise their termination rights to get The Matrix back from Warner Brothers, which is now owned by Trump's cronies, thanks to California Attorney General Rob Bonta's decision to let the Warner-Paramount merger go through: https://puck.news/hollywood/2026/11/the-wachowskis-are-reclaiming-the-matrix This clash between termination and loan-outs has been on my radar since 2021, when the artist-defending media lawyer Jeff Trexler told me about it over drinks at Comic-Con. I've since spoken to accountants and lawyers who think there might be a way to finesse this if creators set up contracts with their loan-outs that give the loan-outs the right to collect their royalties and advances, without assigning copyright to the loan-out companies. I don't have any definitive answers on this: if you're worried about it, you should talk to your own lawyers and accountants. It's a dangerous erosion of one of the few bright spots in copyright, a rule that is an unambiguously good way to benefit artists, not media companies. In the meantime, if you've got some 35-year-old copyrights you'd like to terminate, I've got a tip for you.
